def corr_heatmap(df, title, figsize=(11, 9)):
    """Annotated correlation heatmap of the numeric columns of df."""
    corr = df.corr(numeric_only=True)
    cols = corr.columns
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    im = ax.imshow(corr, cmap='RdBu_r', vmin=-1, vmax=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(cols)))
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(cols)))
    ax.set_xticklabels(cols, rotation=90)
    ax.set_yticklabels(cols)
    for i in range(len(cols)):
        for j in range(len(cols)):
            ax.text(j, i, f'{corr.iloc[i, j]:.2f}', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7,
                    color='white' if abs(corr.iloc[i, j]) > 0.6 else 'black')
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label='Correlation')
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    return corr


def strongest_pairs(corr, n_pos=8, n_neg=5):
    """Strongest pairwise correlations, excluding the diagonal."""
    pairs = corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape, dtype=bool), k=1)).stack().sort_values(ascending=False)
    print("Strongest positive correlations:")
    display(pairs.head(n_pos).round(3))
    print("Strongest negative correlations:")
    display(pairs.tail(n_neg).round(3))

Comment (c). The data set has 777 colleges and 18 variables, none missing. Most count variables are strongly right-skewed: Apps has median 1 558 but mean 3 002 and maximum 48 094, and the same holds for Accept, Enroll, F.Undergrad and P.Undergrad, so a few very large universities pull the means far above the medians. Outstate ranges from 2 340 to 21 700 dollars with median 9 990. Two values are impossible: Grad.Rate has a maximum of 118 % and PhD a maximum of 103 %, which must be data entry errors. Median S.F.Ratio is 13.6 students per faculty member and median Grad.Rate is 65 %.

(d) Scatterplot matrix of Top10perc, Apps, Enroll.

In [223]:
columns = ["Top10perc", "Apps", "Enroll"]
pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(college[columns])
plt.show()

Comment (d). Apps and Enroll are strongly positively related, as expected since enrolment is bounded by applications, and the relationship is roughly linear with a few large state universities in the upper right. Top10perc has a weaker, positive but noisy relationship with both: colleges with many top-10 % students receive more applications, but there are many small selective colleges with few applications. The diagonal histograms confirm the right skew seen in (c).

(e) Outstate versus Private.

In [224]:
college.boxplot(column='Outstate', by='Private')
plt.show()

Comment (e). Private colleges charge clearly more out-of-state tuition: the median is roughly 11 000 dollars for private colleges against roughly 6 600 dollars for public ones, and the interquartile ranges barely overlap. Private colleges also show a much wider spread, from about 2 300 to 21 700 dollars, whereas public colleges are concentrated in a narrow band. Public colleges are largely state-funded, so out-of-state tuition does not need to cover the full cost.

(f) Elite universities: more than 50 % of new students from the top 10 % of their high school class.

Comment (f). Note that Top10perc is measured in percent, so the cut points are 50 and 100 rather than the book's 0.5 and 1 (with the book's values only 3 colleges would be classified). With the correct cut points 78 of 777 colleges (10 %) are elite. Elite colleges have much higher out-of-state tuition, median about 15 000 dollars against about 10 000 dollars, and the lower quartile of the elite group lies above the median of the non-elite group.

Comment (g). Apps is extremely right-skewed: most colleges receive fewer than 5 000 applications and a long tail reaches 48 000, so with 20 bins almost all mass sits in the first two. Outstate is roughly symmetric and bimodal-looking with 10 bins, reflecting the public/private split seen in (e). PhD is left-skewed with most colleges between 60 and 95 %. Grad.Rate is approximately symmetric around 65 % but the 15-bin histogram shows the impossible value above 100. Changing the number of bins mostly changes how much detail is visible; too few bins hide the bimodality of Outstate, too many make Apps look like a single spike.

Summary of (h).

  • Elite versus non-elite. Elite colleges receive more than twice as many applications but accept a much smaller share (acceptance rate 0.54 against 0.77). They charge more (Outstate 15 200 against 9 900 dollars), spend about twice as much per student (Expend 18 400 against 8 700), have fewer students per faculty member (10.6 against 14.5), more faculty with a PhD, far fewer part-time students, more alumni who donate (34 % against 21 %) and a much higher graduation rate (83 % against 63 %).
  • Private versus public. Private colleges are only marginally more selective on average (acceptance rate 0.75 against 0.73) but much more heterogeneous: both the most and the least selective colleges are private. 65 of the 78 elite colleges are private. Private colleges have a lower student/faculty ratio and, as seen in (e), much higher tuition.
  • Graduation rate. Grad.Rate correlates most strongly with Outstate (0.57), Top10perc (0.50) and perc.alumni (0.49), and negatively with S.F.Ratio (−0.31), acceptance rate (−0.29), Personal (−0.27) and P.Undergrad (−0.26). Colleges with well-prepared, full-time students and more resources graduate more of them. These are associations, not causal effects: expensive colleges recruit students who are already likely to graduate.
  • Multicollinearity. Three groups of variables measure almost the same thing: size (Apps, Accept, Enroll, F.Undergrad, correlations 0.81 to 0.97), selectivity (Top10perc and Top25perc, 0.89) and faculty qualification (PhD and Terminal, 0.85). In a regression one variable per group would suffice. The strongest negative correlations all involve S.F.Ratio, against Expend (−0.58) and Outstate (−0.56): well-funded colleges have small classes.
  • Data quality. Cazenovia College has Grad.Rate 118 % and Texas A&M at Galveston has PhD 103 %; both should be treated as errors.

(c) Pairwise relationships between the predictors.

In [231]:
corr = corr_heatmap(Boston, 'Correlation matrix, Boston')
In [232]:
# Point size = number of observations sharing the same (x, y); clusters with n >= 20 are labelled
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8))
pairs = [
    ('tax', 'rad', 'Property-tax rate', 'Accessibility to radial highways'),
    ('lstat', 'medv', 'Lower status of population (%)', 'Median home value'),
    ('indus', 'nox', 'Non-retail business acres (%)', 'NOx concentration'),
    ('medv', 'ptratio', 'Median home value', 'Pupil-teacher ratio'),
]
for ax, (x, y, xlab, ylab) in zip(axes.ravel(), pairs):
    counts = Boston.groupby([x, y]).size().reset_index(name='n')
    ax.scatter(counts[x], counts[y], s=8 + 4*counts['n'], alpha=0.4,
               edgecolor='k', linewidth=0.3)
    for _, r in counts[counts['n'] >= 20].iterrows():
        ax.annotate(f"n={int(r['n'])}", (r[x], r[y]),
                    textcoords='offset points', xytext=(8, -12), fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlab); ax.set_ylabel(ylab)
    ax.set_title(f'{y} vs {x}', fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Comment (c). The correlation matrix and the scatterplots show a few strong structures. rad and tax are highly correlated (0.91), but the scatterplot reveals why: a single cluster of 132 suburbs shares the values rad = 24 and tax = 666, so the correlation is driven by one block of suburbs rather than by a smooth relationship. medv decreases with lstat in a clearly non-linear, convex way, and medv is censored at 50, visible as a row of points at the top. nox rises with indus up to about 18 % non-retail acres, where another large vertical cluster sits (indus = 18.1 is the same block of suburbs). ptratio shows a weak negative relationship with medv, and several horizontal bands appear because the ratio is set per town. Many variables are therefore shared by groups of suburbs, which produces repeated values and clusters rather than continuous clouds.

Comment (d). Per capita crime is most strongly associated with rad (0.63) and tax (0.58): suburbs with high highway accessibility and high property-tax rates have more crime, but this is mostly the block of 132 suburbs with rad = 24 and tax = 666, which are also the ones with indus = 18.1. lstat (0.46), nox (0.42), indus (0.41) and age (0.35) are positively associated: older, more industrial, more polluted suburbs with a poorer population have more crime. medv (−0.39) and dis (−0.38) are negatively associated: crime is lower where homes are more valuable and further from the employment centres. The relationships are far from linear, since crim is extremely skewed (see (e)).

(e) Range of crim, tax and ptratio.

Comment (e). crim ranges from 0.006 to 88.98 with median 0.26 and mean 3.61, so the distribution is extremely right-skewed: half of the suburbs have essentially no crime, but 66 suburbs lie above the IQR outlier limit and a handful have rates above 40. tax ranges from 187 to 711 with a clear gap: the bulk lies between 187 and about 470, and then a block of suburbs sits at 666, which is why the histogram is bimodal and no point counts as an outlier. ptratio ranges from 12.6 to 22, is left-skewed with a large spike at 20.2, and has no outliers. So yes: some suburbs have particularly high crime rates, a large block has a high tax rate, and pupil-teacher ratios are high but within a narrow range.

Comment (i). 64 suburbs average more than seven rooms per dwelling and 13 average more than eight. The 13 large-dwelling suburbs are wealthy: the median home value is 48 300 dollars against 21 200 overall, and four of them hit the 50 000 censoring limit. They have much lower lstat (4.1 % against 11.4 %), a lower pupil-teacher ratio (17.4 against 19.05), less industry (6.2 against 9.7) and somewhat lower tax. Crime is slightly higher than the overall median (0.52 against 0.26) but still low. One exception is suburb 364, which has rm = 8.78 but medv only 21.9, with rad = 24, tax = 666 and ptratio = 20.2, so it belongs to the high-tax block and large homes there are not worth as much.

Comment (a).

  • i. Yes. The coefficient of horsepower has t = −24.5 and p-value < 0.0001, so the null hypothesis of no relationship is rejected. The F-statistic of 600 says the same thing.
  • ii. The relationship is fairly strong: R² = 0.606, so horsepower alone explains about 61 % of the variance of mpg. The residual standard error is 4.9 mpg against a mean mpg of 23.4, about 21 %.
  • iii. Negative. Each additional horsepower is associated with 0.158 fewer miles per gallon on average.
  • iv. At horsepower = 98 the predicted mpg is 39.94 − 0.158 × 98 = 24.47. The intervals are computed in the next cell.

Confidence and prediction interval at horsepower = 98, computed by hand and checked against statsmodels.

In [238]:
def get_residual_se(y_true, y_pred, df):
    # RSS = Sum of squared residual errors
    RSS = ((y_true - y_pred) ** 2).sum()
    s = (RSS / df) ** 0.5
    return s


def get_pred_se(x, x0, CI=True):
    n = len(x)
    x_mean = sum(x) / n
    s_xx = sum((x - x_mean) ** 2)

    if CI:
        inside = (1 / n) + ((x0 - x_mean) ** 2) / s_xx 
    else:
        inside = (
            1 + (1 / n) + ((x0 - x_mean) ** 2) / s_xx
        )  

    return inside**0.5


def get_CI(x0, ci_level, p, data, x_col, y_col, model):
    n = len(data)  
    df = n - p
    alpha = 1 - ci_level

    y_0_hat = model.predict([1.0, x0])[0]
    t_crit = float(t.ppf(1 - alpha / 2, df=df))

    s = get_residual_se(data[y_col], model.fittedvalues, df)
    scale_factor = get_pred_se(data[x_col], x0, CI=True)  

    margin = t_crit * s * scale_factor
    return [float(y_0_hat - margin), float(y_0_hat + margin)]


def get_PI(x0, ci_level, p, data, x_col, y_col, model):
    n = len(data)  
    df = n - p
    alpha = 1 - ci_level

    y_0_hat = model.predict([1.0, x0])[0]
    t_crit = float(t.ppf(1 - alpha / 2, df=df))

    s = get_residual_se(data[y_col], model.fittedvalues, df)
    scale_factor = get_pred_se(data[x_col], x0, CI=False)  

    margin = t_crit * s * scale_factor
    return [float(y_0_hat - margin), float(y_0_hat + margin)]


# Evaluate at horsepower = 98
x0 = 98
ci = get_CI(
    x0,
    ci_level=0.95,
    p=2,
    data=auto,
    x_col='horsepower',
    y_col='mpg',
    model=lin_reg,
)
pi = get_PI(
    x0,
    ci_level=0.95,
    p=2,
    data=auto,
    x_col='horsepower',
    y_col='mpg',
    model=lin_reg,
)

print(f'95% CI for x0={x0}: {ci}')
print(f'95% PI for x0={x0}: {pi}')

# Check against statsmodels
display(lin_reg.get_prediction(np.array([[1.0, x0]])).summary_frame(alpha=0.05).round(3))

Comment (a) iv. The 95 % confidence interval for the mean mpg of cars with 98 horsepower is [23.97, 24.96], and the 95 % prediction interval for a single car is [14.81, 34.12]. The hand computation using the formulas $\hat y_0 \pm t_{n-2}\, s\sqrt{1/n + (x_0-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}}$ and $\hat y_0 \pm t_{n-2}\, s\sqrt{1 + 1/n + (x_0-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}}$ agrees with statsmodels to all shown decimals. The prediction interval is about ten times wider than the confidence interval because it also includes the irreducible error of an individual car, not only the uncertainty in the fitted line.

(b) Scatterplot with the least squares line.

In [239]:
def abline(ax, b, m, *args, **kwargs):
    "Add a line with slope m and intercept b to ax"
    xlim = ax.get_xlim()
    ylim = [m * xlim[0] + b, m * xlim[1] + b]
    ax.plot(xlim, ylim, *args, **kwargs)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
ax.scatter(auto['horsepower'], auto['mpg'], alpha=0.5)
abline(ax, lin_reg.params['const'], lin_reg.params['horsepower'], 'r--', linewidth=2)
ax.set_xlabel('horsepower'); ax.set_ylabel('mpg')
plt.show()

Comment (b). The least squares line captures the downward trend, but the points are clearly curved around it: cars with very low and very high horsepower lie mostly above the line, and cars in the middle range (around 100 to 150 hp) lie mostly below it. A straight line is therefore not the right functional form; mpg decreases quickly at first and then flattens out.

# Binned residuals: is the mean residual zero and the spread constant across horsepower?
x = auto['horsepower']
bins = pd.qcut(x, 10)
g = resid.groupby(bins, observed=True)
summ = pd.DataFrame({'center': x.groupby(bins, observed=True).mean(),
                     'mean': g.mean(), 'sd': g.std(), 'n': g.size()})
summ['se'] = summ['sd'] / np.sqrt(summ['n'])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
axes[0].scatter(x, resid, alpha=0.2, color='grey')
axes[0].errorbar(summ['center'], summ['mean'], yerr=2*summ['se'], fmt='o-', color='k', capsize=3)
axes[0].axhline(0, color='r', ls='--')
axes[0].set(xlabel='horsepower', ylabel='residual', title='Binned mean residual ±2 SE')
axes[1].plot(summ['center'], summ['sd'], 'o-')
axes[1].set(xlabel='horsepower', ylabel='residual SD', title='Residual spread per bin')
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Comment (c). The residual plots reveal three problems.

  • Non-linearity. The residuals versus horsepower and versus fitted values form a U-shape: positive for low and high horsepower, negative in the middle. The binned means confirm this, being significantly above zero at about 60 hp, significantly below zero between 95 and 150 hp, and above zero again at about 185 hp. A quadratic term or a log transformation of horsepower would fix this.
  • Non-constant variance. The residual spread decreases with horsepower: the standard deviation per bin falls from about 5.6 at 60 hp to about 2 to 3.5 above 130 hp. Since mpg is more variable among small cars, a log transformation of mpg would stabilise the variance.
  • Non-normality. The histogram and Q-Q plot show a right-skewed residual distribution with a heavier upper tail (skew 0.49, Jarque-Bera p = 0.0002). This is mild and mostly a consequence of the curvature.

The Durbin-Watson statistic of 0.92 also indicates positive autocorrelation, but this reflects the ordering of the data (cars are roughly sorted by year and make) rather than a time series problem.

The scatterplot matrix shows that all four negative relationships are curved, as in Exercise 8. The four engine-size variables are also very strongly correlated with each other, from 0.84 to 0.95, so they carry almost the same information and multicollinearity is to be expected in the multiple regression. cylinders, year and origin are discrete and appear as vertical bands.

Comment (c).

  • i. Yes. The F-statistic is 252 with p-value 2 × 10⁻¹³⁹, so at least one predictor is related to mpg. The model explains 82 % of the variance (R² = 0.821), a large improvement over the 61 % from horsepower alone.
  • ii. weight (p < 0.001), year (p < 0.001), origin (p < 0.001) and displacement (p = 0.008) are statistically significant. cylinders, horsepower and acceleration are not, although horsepower was highly significant on its own. This is the multicollinearity seen in (b): once weight and displacement are in the model, horsepower and cylinders add little independent information, which is also flagged by the large condition number. The sign of displacement is even positive, which should not be interpreted causally.
  • iii. The coefficient of year is 0.75: holding the other variables fixed, each model year is associated with 0.75 more miles per gallon, so fuel efficiency improved by about 7.5 mpg over the decade 1970 to 1982 for cars of the same size and power. origin is coded 1 = American, 2 = European, 3 = Japanese and is treated as numeric here; its coefficient of 1.43 says that European and Japanese cars get more mpg than American cars of the same specification.

(d) Diagnostic plots (the four plots of R's plot(lm)).

In [244]:
def diagnostic_plots(results, n_label=3):
    """The four plots of R's plot(lm) for a fitted statsmodels OLS result."""
    infl = results.get_influence()
    fitted, resid = results.fittedvalues, results.resid
    std_resid = infl.resid_studentized_internal
    leverage, cooks = infl.hat_matrix_diag, infl.cooks_distance[0]
    p, n = results.df_model + 1, len(resid)
    idx = results.model.data.row_labels
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 9))

    # 1. Residuals vs fitted: curvature = wrong functional form
    ax = axes[0, 0]
    ax.scatter(fitted, resid, alpha=0.5)
    s = lowess(resid, fitted, frac=0.6); ax.plot(s[:, 0], s[:, 1], 'r-')
    ax.axhline(0, color='grey', ls='--')
    ax.set(xlabel='Fitted values', ylabel='Residuals Fitted')
    for i in np.argsort(np.abs(resid.values))[-n_label:]:
        ax.annotate(idx[i], (fitted.iloc[i], resid.iloc[i]), fontsize=8)

    # 2. Normal Q-Q of standardized residuals
    ax = axes[0, 1]
    (osm, osr), (slope, intercept, _) = stats.probplot(std_resid, dist='norm')
    ax.scatter(osm, osr, alpha=0.5); ax.plot(osm, slope*osm + intercept, 'r-')
    ax.set(xlabel='Theoretical quantiles', ylabel='Standardized residuals', title='Normal Q-Q')

    # 3. Scale-location: trend = non-constant v
    ax = axes[1, 0]
    sqrt_abs = np.sqrt(np.abs(std_resid))
    ax.scatter(fitted, sqrt_abs, alpha=0.5)
    s = lowess(sqrt_abs, fitted, frac=0.6); ax.plot(s[:, 0], s[:, 1], 'r-')
    ax.set(xlabel='Fitted values', ylabel=r'$\sqrt{|\mathrm{std.\ residuals}|}$', title='Scale-Location')

    # 4. Residuals vs leverage with Cook's distance contours
    ax = axes[1, 1]
    ax.scatter(leverage, std_resid, alpha=0.5)
    ax.axhline(0, color='grey', ls='--')
    ax.axvline(2*p/n, color='grey', ls=':', label='2p/n')
    lev = np.linspace(leverage.min(), leverage.max(), 100)
    for d in (0.5, 1.0):
        for sign in (1, -1):
            ax.plot(lev, sign*np.sqrt(d*p*(1 - lev)/lev), 'r--', lw=0.8)
    ax.set_ylim(std_resid.min() - 0.5, std_resid.max() + 0.5)
    ax.set(xlabel='Leverage', ylabel='Standardized residuals', title="Residuals vs Leverage")
    for i in np.argsort(cooks)[-n_label:]:
        ax.annotate(idx[i], (leverage[i], std_resid[i]), fontsize=8)
    ax.legend()
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

diagnostic_plots(results)
plt.show()

Comment (d). The four diagnostic plots show the same non-linearity as in the simple regression: the residuals versus fitted values are U-shaped, with large positive residuals for the most efficient cars (fitted values above 30). The scale-location plot shows a mildly increasing spread with the fitted value. The Q-Q plot is close to the line except in the upper tail, where about ten standardized residuals lie above 2.9; the largest are mazda glc (3.95), vw dasher (diesel) (3.63) and vw rabbit c (diesel) (3.45), all small, mostly diesel cars whose fuel efficiency the linear model underestimates. These are unusually large residuals but none exceeds 4, so they are moderate outliers. In the leverage plot, buick estate wagon (sw) has by far the highest leverage, 0.19 against the threshold 2p/n = 0.04, because it combines the heaviest weight with a large engine; its standardized residual is only −1.6 and its Cook's distance 0.08, so it is a high-leverage point but not an influential one. vw pickup and vw dasher (diesel) combine leverage slightly above the threshold with large residuals, but their Cook's distances are below 0.06, so no single observation drives the fit.

Comment (e). Every interaction tried is statistically significant, which is not surprising with 392 observations. The two most useful are horsepower:weight and displacement:horsepower, which each raise the adjusted R² from 0.818 to about 0.86. In the model mpg ~ horsepower * weight + year + origin all terms are significant, and the interaction coefficient is positive (5.5 × 10⁻⁵, p < 0.001): the penalty of extra horsepower on mpg is smaller for heavy cars than for light cars, or equivalently the effect of weight is weaker for powerful cars. This model with five terms has a higher adjusted R² (0.859) than the full additive model with seven predictors, and it drops the collinear cylinders, displacement and acceleration. The residuals remain right-skewed, so the interaction does not remove the non-linearity completely.

(f) Transformations of the variables.

  'base':        base,

  'log(hp)':     base.replace('horsepower', 'np.log(horsepower)'),
  'sqrt(hp)':    base.replace('horsepower', 'np.sqrt(horsepower)'),
  'log(mpg)':    'np.log(mpg) ~ cylinders + displacement + horsepower + weight + acceleration + year + origin',
  'log-log':     'np.log(mpg) ~ cylinders + displacement + np.log(horsepower) + np.log(weight) + acceleration + year + origin',
}
for name, f in models.items():
    m = ols(f, auto).fit()

Comment (f). Transforming horsepower improves the fit: a quadratic term raises the adjusted R² from 0.818 to 0.852, log(horsepower) to 0.834 and the square root to 0.824. All of these still fail the Breusch-Pagan test (p < 0.001), so the variance of the residuals remains non-constant. Transforming the response works better: log(mpg) gives adjusted R² 0.877 and a Breusch-Pagan p-value of 0.09, and the log-log model with log(horsepower) and log(weight) gives the best fit, adjusted R² 0.889, with p = 0.13 for the Breusch-Pagan test, so heteroscedasticity is no longer detected. The log transformation of mpg makes sense physically, since fuel consumption per mile (1/mpg) is closer to proportional to weight and power, and it turns the multiplicative relationship into an additive one. The recommended model is therefore log(mpg) on log(horsepower), log(weight), year and origin.

Additional coding task: bias-variance trade-off¶

Setup¶

The ground truth is $$ f(x) = \sin(2x_1), \qquad y = f(x) + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),\ \sigma = 0.5 . $$ There are $p$ predictors $x = (x_1, \dots, x_p)$, each drawn independently from $\mathcal{U}(-1, 1)$, but only $x_1$ carries information about $y$; the remaining $p - 1$ predictors are pure noise. We use a fixed design with $n_{\text{train}} = 50$ training points and $n_{\text{test}} = 500$ noise-free test points $\{(x_0, f(x_0))\}$, and vary $p \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 20\}$.

Two estimators $\hat f$ are compared:

  • Linear regression $\hat f(x) = \hat\beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^p \hat\beta_j x_j$, fitted by least squares.
  • KNN regression $\hat f(x_0) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in N_K(x_0)} y_i$, where $N_K(x_0)$ are the $K$ training points closest to $x_0$ in Euclidean distance over all $p$ predictors, for $K = 1, \dots, 9$.

Bias-variance decomposition¶

For a fixed test point $x_0$ and a training set $\mathcal{D}$ (here: fixed $X$, random noise $\varepsilon$), the expected squared error of $\hat f$ against the true function decomposes as $$ \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\Big[\big(f(x_0) - \hat f(x_0; \mathcal{D})\big)^2\Big] = \underbrace{\big(f(x_0) - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\hat f(x_0)]\big)^2}_{\text{Bias}^2(x_0)} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\Big[\big(\hat f(x_0) - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\hat f(x_0)]\big)^2\Big]}_{\text{Var}(x_0)} . $$ The cross term vanishes because $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\big[\hat f(x_0) - \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\hat f(x_0)]\big] = 0$. If the test response were observed with noise, the irreducible error $\sigma^2 = 0.25$ would be added; since we compare with $f(x_0)$ directly it is left out, so $\text{MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Var}$ holds exactly.

Monte Carlo estimation¶

The expectation over $\mathcal{D}$ is approximated by drawing $L = 100$ independent noise vectors $\varepsilon^{(l)}$, refitting the model on $y^{(l)} = f(X) + \varepsilon^{(l)}$ each time, and predicting at every test point. Writing $\hat f^{(l)}(x_0)$ for the prediction from replication $l$, $$ \bar f(x_0) = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L} \hat f^{(l)}(x_0) $$ estimates $\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\hat f(x_0)]$. Averaging over the $n_{\text{test}}$ test points gives the three reported quantities: $$ \widehat{\text{Bias}^2} = \frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}} \sum_{x_0} \big(f(x_0) - \bar f(x_0)\big)^2, \qquad \widehat{\text{Var}} = \frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}} \sum_{x_0} \frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L} \big(\hat f^{(l)}(x_0) - \bar f(x_0)\big)^2, \qquad \widehat{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}} \sum_{x_0} \frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L} \big(\hat f^{(l)}(x_0) - f(x_0)\big)^2 . $$ In the code, yhat_lm and yhat_knn[:, :, j] are the $n_{\text{test}} \times L$ matrices of $\hat f^{(l)}(x_0)$, ybar_* is $\bar f(x_0)$, biasSQ_*, variance_* and err_* are the three estimates above, and the results are collected in out_lm (one row per $p$) and out_knn (one row per $(p, K)$).

What to expect¶

  • KNN, effect of $K$. Small $K$ averages few noisy responses, so $\text{Var} \approx \sigma^2 / K$ is large and the bias is small: a flexible fit. Large $K$ averages over a wide neighbourhood in which $f$ is not constant, so the bias grows while the variance shrinks. The MSE is U-shaped in $1/K$.
  • KNN, effect of $p$. With more noise predictors the Euclidean distance is dominated by irrelevant coordinates, so the $K$ nearest neighbours are no longer close in $x_1$ and the local average is taken over points with very different $f$ values. This inflates the bias for every $K$: the curse of dimensionality.
  • Linear regression. $\hat f$ is linear but $f$ is a sine, so there is a model bias that does not depend on $p$. Each noise predictor adds one coefficient estimated from 50 points, so the variance grows roughly linearly in $p$, approximately $\sigma^2 (p+1)/n_{\text{train}}$.
  • The MSE pattern should resemble FIGURE 3.20 in the book: KNN is competitive for $p \le 2$ and linear regression wins for larger $p$.
In [ ]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

ntrain = 50  # Training
ntest = 500  # Test
nrep = 100  # Repeat 100 times
p = 20
puse = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 20])  # Number of predictors
k = np.arange(1, 10)

sigma = 0.5
np.random.seed(0)
Xtrain = np.random.uniform(-1, 1, [ntrain, p])
Xtest = np.random.uniform(-1, 1, [ntest, p])
y0 = np.sin(2 * Xtrain[:, 0])  # Only the first predictor is related to y
ytest = np.sin(2 * Xtest[:, 0])

out_knn = pd.DataFrame()  # Output results
out_lm = pd.DataFrame()

for i in range(len(puse)):
    yhat_lm = np.zeros((ntest, nrep))
    yhat_knn = np.zeros((ntest, nrep, len(k)))
    
    for l in range(nrep):
        y = y0 + np.random.normal(0, sigma, ntrain)
    
        ######### DO: fit linear regression using LinearRegression funciton, assign predicted value to yhat_lm[:, [l]] #########
        fit_lm = LinearRegression().fit(Xtrain[:, :puse[i]], y)
        yhat_lm[:, l] =  fit_lm.predict(Xtest[:, :puse[i]])
    
        for j in range(len(k)):
            
            ######### DO: fit knn using KNeighborsRegressor funciton, assign predicted value to yhat_knn[:, l, j] #########
            fit_knn = KNeighborsRegressor(k[j]).fit(Xtrain[:, :puse[i]], y)
            yhat_knn[:, l, j] = fit_knn.predict(Xtest[:, :puse[i]])
        
        
        #print(i + 1, "-th p, ", l + 1, "-th repetition finished. \n")
    
  
    ######### DO: compute bias and variance of linear regression #########
    
    # Compute mean of predicted values
    ybar_lm = yhat_lm.mean(axis=1)
    
    # Compute bias^2
    biasSQ_lm = np.mean((ytest - ybar_lm)**2)
    
    # Compute variance
    variance_lm = np.mean((yhat_lm - ybar_lm[:, None])**2)
    
    # Compute total MSE
    err_lm = np.mean((yhat_lm - ytest[:, None])**2)

    out_lm = pd.concat([out_lm, pd.DataFrame({'biasSQ_lm': [biasSQ_lm], 'variance_lm': [variance_lm], 'MSE': [err_lm], 'p': [puse[i]]})])
    out_lm = out_lm.reset_index(drop=True)
    
    ######### DO: compute bias and variance of knn regression #########
    for j in range(len(k)):
        yh = yhat_knn[:, :, j]
        # Compute mean of predicted values
        ybar_knn = yh.mean(axis=1)

        # Compute bias^2
        biasSQ_knn = np.mean((ytest - ybar_knn)**2)
    

        # Compute variance
        variance_knn = np.mean((yh - ybar_knn[:, None])**2)

        # Compute total MSE
        err_knn = np.mean((yh - ytest[:, None])**2)

        out_knn = pd.concat([out_knn, pd.DataFrame({'biasSQ_knn': [biasSQ_knn], 'variance_knn': [variance_knn], 'MSE': [err_knn], '1/K': [1 / k[j]], 'p': [puse[i]]})])
        out_knn = out_knn.reset_index(drop=True)

for ax, pv in zip(axes.ravel(), puse):
    d = out_knn[out_knn['p'] == pv].sort_values('1/K')
    lm = out_lm.loc[out_lm['p'] == pv, 'MSE'].iloc[0]
    ax.plot(d['1/K'], d['MSE'], 'o-', color='green', label='KNN')
    ax.axhline(lm, color='k', ls='--', label='Linear regression')
    ax.set_xscale('log'); ax.set_title(f'p = {pv}')
    ax.set_xlabel('1/K'); ax.set_ylabel('Mean squared error')
axes[0, 0].legend(); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for ax, pv in zip(axes.ravel(), puse):

    ax.plot(d['1/K'], d['biasSQ_knn'], 'o-', label='Bias$^2$')
    ax.plot(d['1/K'], d['variance_knn'], 's-', label='Variance')

    ax.set_xscale('log'); ax.set_title(f'KNN, p = {pv}'); ax.set_xlabel('1/K')
axes[0, 0].legend(); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

ax.plot(out_lm['p'], out_lm['biasSQ_lm'], 'o-', label='Bias$^2$')
ax.plot(out_lm['p'], out_lm['variance_lm'], 's-', label='Variance')
ax.plot(out_lm['p'], out_lm['MSE'], 'k^-', label='MSE')

Discussion¶

Linear regression. The squared bias is almost constant, 0.028 for $p = 1$ to $4$ and rising only to 0.054 at $p = 20$, because the linear fit cannot capture $\sin(2x_1)$ regardless of how many noise predictors are added. The variance grows almost linearly with $p$: 0.010, 0.015, 0.018, 0.026, 0.070 and 0.178 for $p = 1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 20$, close to the theoretical $\sigma^2(p+1)/n = 0.25 \,(p+1)/50$, which gives 0.010 at $p = 1$ and 0.105 at $p = 20$. The total MSE therefore rises from 0.038 to 0.233, driven entirely by variance. The decomposition $\text{MSE} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Var}$ holds to four decimals in every row, as it should since the test targets are noise-free.

KNN, effect of $K$. For every $p$ the variance decreases with $K$ almost exactly as $\sigma^2 / K$: about 0.245 at $K = 1$, 0.125 at $K = 2$ and 0.028 at $K = 9$, and it hardly depends on $p$ at all. The squared bias moves the other way but much more weakly over $K = 1$ to $9$, so within this range the MSE is minimised at large $K$ (the optimal $K$ is 8 or 9 for most $p$, and 6 for $p = 4$). The U-shape in $1/K$ is therefore visible only at its right-hand side, where $K = 1$ and $K = 2$ are clearly worst.

KNN, effect of $p$: the curse of dimensionality. The squared bias at the best $K$ explodes as noise predictors are added: 0.002 for $p = 1$, 0.013 for $p = 2$, 0.05 for $p = 3$, 0.09 for $p = 4$, 0.31 for $p = 10$ and 0.37 for $p = 20$. With $p = 20$ the bias alone exceeds the variance of the training noise, because the "nearest" neighbours in 20 dimensions are essentially random points in $x_1$, so the local average is close to the global mean of $f$, which is zero. The best achievable KNN MSE rises from 0.032 at $p = 1$ to 0.384 at $p = 20$, a twelvefold increase, while the variance is unchanged.

Comparison. With $p = 1$ KNN with $K = 9$ (MSE 0.032) beats linear regression (0.038), because the sine is non-linear and one dimension is enough for neighbours to be genuinely close. At $p = 2$ the two are roughly tied (0.045 against 0.042). From $p = 3$ onward linear regression wins for every $K$, and at $p = 20$ its MSE of 0.23 is well below the best KNN value of 0.38. Linear regression pays for extra noise predictors with variance that grows linearly, whereas KNN pays with bias that grows much faster. This reproduces the pattern of FIGURE 3.20: a parametric model with a wrong but reasonable functional form is more robust to irrelevant predictors than a non-parametric one, and the advantage of flexibility disappears as soon as the effective dimension of the problem is larger than one or two.
